title: India's First Hydrogen-Powered Train Crosses 1,200 km in Trials, Saves 3,200 Litres of Diesel
excerpt: The indigenous 10-coach train running between Jind and Sonipat emits only water vapour, with Delhi trials set to begin soon.
body:
• India's first hydrogen-powered train has completed over 1,200 km of trial operations between Jind and Sonipat in Haryana, saving 3,200 litres of diesel
  • The 10-coach indigenous train produces only water vapour as a direct emission, with two hydrogen driving power cars delivering 2,400 kW total power
  • India has built the country's first integrated hydrogen railway ecosystem at Jind, including production, storage and refuelling infrastructure
  • Trials on the Delhi route will begin soon, with India joining Germany, Japan, Sweden and China among nations operating hydrogen rail systems

India's first hydrogen-powered train has crossed a major milestone, completing more than 1,200 kilometres of trial operations while replacing 3,200 litres of diesel with nothing but water vapour as its exhaust. The achievement places India among a small but growing group of nations deploying hydrogen fuel cell technology on their railways.

How the Train Works

The 10-coach train generates electricity onboard through a chemical reaction between hydrogen and oxygen. The process produces electricity to power the train's motors while emitting only water vapour and heat — no smoke, no carbon, no particulate matter. It is the cleanest form of rail propulsion currently available.

https://x.com/MeghUpdates/status/2081314898517385621

Two hydrogen driving power cars deliver a combined 2,400 kW of power, supported by lithium iron phosphate batteries and hydrogen cylinders. Green hydrogen is stored at pressures up to 500 bar and dispensed at 350 bar. Indian Railways has established a dedicated hydrogen production, storage and refuelling facility at Jind — the country's first integrated hydrogen railway ecosystem.

The train has a design speed of 110 kmph and an operational speed of 75 kmph, with a carrying capacity of approximately 2,600 passengers.

Built in India, for India

Developed under the Make in India initiative, the project was led by the Integral Coach Factory in Chennai and the Research Designs and Standards Organisation, with support from Indian engineering partners. The Railway Board approved the trainset for operation on May 22 after extensive oscillation and safety trials.

"India has retained the intellectual property rights for the indigenous hydrogen train technology, paving the way for future exports."

— Union Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw

Multiple independent safety systems detect leaks, heat, flames and smoke, backed by automatic shut-off mechanisms and continuous ventilation. The system meets international safety standards and has passed all mandatory validation protocols.

What's Next

Following successful operations on the 89-km Jind–Sonipat section of Northern Railway in Haryana, trials on the Delhi route are expected to begin soon, according to the Ministry of Railways. The expansion will test the train's performance on busier corridors with higher traffic density.

Hydrogen-powered trains are particularly suited for non-electrified routes where conventional electrification is difficult or economically unviable. India's vast network of 68,000 route-kilometres includes thousands of kilometres that remain diesel-dependent, making hydrogen a potentially transformative alternative.

The project forms part of Indian Railways' broader strategy to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2030. With the intellectual property fully retained domestically, officials see export potential as countries across Asia and Africa look for affordable clean rail solutions.
